5.3.1.examLens: Decide whether a control is worth what it costs. This is the same money logic as 1.3.3, applied to the cost of keeping the gains.

worked.question: Without controls, a project's $80,000 per year of savings is expected to erode by half. Option 1: an inline sensor and monitoring system costing $30,000 upfront plus $5,000 per year. Option 2: a manual audit costing $12,000 per year that is expected to prevent only $6,000 of that loss. Which options are justified?
worked.solution:
Expected loss without controls = 50% × $80,000 = $40,000 per year.
Option 1: annual net benefit = 40,000 − 5,000 = $35,000. Payback = 30,000 ÷ 35,000 = 0.86 year (about 10 months). Justified.
Option 2: it costs $12,000 per year to protect $6,000, a net loss of $6,000 per year. Not justified.

5.3.2.examLens: Know what a complete control plan contains and spot what is missing.

worked.question: A control plan row reads: Step: boring. Characteristic: bore diameter. Specification: 25.00 ± 0.05 mm. Measurement: caliper. Sample: 5 parts per hour. Control method: Xbar-R chart. Owner: (blank). Reaction plan: (blank). What is wrong?
worked.solution: The owner and the reaction plan are missing. Without an owner nobody is accountable for the chart, and without a reaction plan nobody knows what to do when it signals. It would also be worth confirming that the caliper has been validated (a measurement system analysis), since a caliper may not resolve a ±0.05 mm tolerance well.

5.3.3.examLens: Know the sequence of actions after a signal, and keep out-of-control and out-of-spec apart.

worked.question: Classify each and give the right response: (A) a point beyond the upper control limit, but the part is within spec; (B) the chart is stable but 4% of parts are out of spec; (C) a point beyond the control limit and the part is out of spec.
worked.solution:
(A) Out of control, within spec: a special cause is present. Contain if needed, investigate and correct the cause before it grows.
(B) In control, out of spec: a stable but incapable process. Investigating individual points will not help. Reduce variation, recenter, or redesign the process. Sort or contain the nonconforming output meanwhile.
(C) Both: contain and segregate the part first, then investigate the special cause, correct it, and document the disposition.

5.3.1.a.title: Cost of controls versus the benefit
5.3.1.a.html: Controls are not free. Compare the cost of sustaining them (monitoring, training, audits, inspection, software) with the benefit of preventing the process from sliding back. A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is not worth keeping.

5.3.1.b.title: ROI and payback
5.3.1.b.html:
Use the same tools as in SG-1.3.

  • ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost.
  • Payback = investment ÷ annual benefit (assuming a steady yearly benefit).

5.3.1.c.title: Include everything
5.3.1.c.html: Count both hard and soft benefits, and include ongoing costs, not just the upfront cost. A control with a small purchase price and a large yearly labor cost can be more expensive than it looks.

5.3.1.d.title: Is a costly control justified?
5.3.1.d.html: Compare the expected savings the control protects with the total cost of the control. The expected loss without the control is the savings at risk times the chance they slip away.

5.3.2.a.title: The core elements
5.3.2.a.html:
For each key process step, a control plan lists:

  • the process step
  • the characteristic (CTQ) being controlled
  • the specification or target
  • the measurement system (and that it has been validated)
  • the sample size and frequency
  • the control method (a control chart, a poka-yoke, an SOP)
  • the owner (who is responsible)
  • the reaction plan (what to do when something goes wrong)
  • a document reference (where the procedure lives)

5.3.2.b.title: Supporting items
5.3.2.b.html: SOPs, training, a named process owner, and a transition plan for the handoff from the project team.

5.3.2.c.title: A living document
5.3.2.c.html: The control plan is owned by the process owner and updated as the process changes. It is not filed away at project close.

5.3.2.d.title: Find what is missing
5.3.2.d.html: Check the list above. The most common gaps are a missing reaction plan and a missing owner.

5.3.3.a.title: The elements
5.3.3.a.html:
A response plan covers:

  • the trigger (an out-of-control signal or a rule violation)
  • immediate containment (stop bad product moving on)
  • who acts
  • investigation to find the cause
  • corrective action
  • escalation if it cannot be resolved quickly
  • documentation
  • resuming normal operation

5.3.3.b.title: Disposition of out-of-spec product
5.3.3.b.html: The plan states the rules for handling nonconforming product: segregate it, then decide to sort, rework, scrap, or accept as is, with named authority for each decision.

5.3.3.c.title: What follows a signal?
5.3.3.c.html: Contain, investigate, correct, document. Containing comes first so that suspect product does not reach the customer.

5.3.3.d.title: Out of control is not out of spec
5.3.3.d.html:
• A point can signal a special cause while still within the spec. Investigate the cause even though the part would pass.
  • A stable process can still produce out-of-spec output if its natural variation is too wide or off target.

The responses differ: investigate a special cause, versus redesign or improve the process itself.

5.3.1-1.stem: A manual audit costs $12,000 per year and is expected to prevent only $6,000 per year of lost savings. Is it justified?

options.html: Yes, because audits are always worthwhile
No; it costs twice what it protects, a net loss of $6,000 per year
Yes, because it prevents some loss

5.3.1-1.explanation: A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is not worth keeping.

5.3.1-2.stem: An inline sensor system costs $30,000 upfront plus $5,000 per year. It protects savings that would otherwise erode by an expected $40,000 per year. What is the payback period on the upfront cost, using the annual net benefit?
5.3.1-2.explanation: Annual net benefit = 40,000 − 5,000 = $35,000. Payback = 30,000 ÷ 35,000 = 0.86 years, about 10 months.

5.3.1-3.stem: When evaluating a control, ongoing costs such as monitoring labor should be included along with the upfront cost.
5.3.1-3.explanation: A control with a small purchase price and a large yearly labor cost can cost more than it appears.

5.3.2-1.stem: A control plan row lists the step, the characteristic (bore diameter), the specification, the measurement tool, the sample size and frequency, and the control method (an Xbar-R chart). The owner and the reaction plan are blank. What is wrong?

options.html: Nothing; owners and reaction plans are optional
Nobody is accountable for the chart and nobody knows what to do when it signals
The sample size is too large

5.3.2-1.explanation: A complete control plan names an owner and a reaction plan for each control.

5.3.2-2.stem: A control plan is finished and closed once the project is presented, and it need not be updated afterward.
5.3.2-2.explanation: A control plan is a living document, owned by the process owner and updated as the process changes.

5.3.2-3.stem: Which TWO are normal elements of a control plan?

options.html: The list of all brainstormed causes

5.3.2-3.explanation: A control plan covers what is controlled, how, how often, who owns it, and what to do when it goes wrong.

5.3.2-4.stem: Which items support a control plan at handoff?

options.html: SOPs, training, a named process owner, and a transition plan

5.3.2-4.explanation: These supporting items help the process owner keep the gains in place.

5.3.3-1.stem: A control chart signals a special cause. What is the correct order of actions?
5.3.3-1.explanation: Contain first so suspect product does not reach the customer, then investigate, correct, and document.

5.3.3-2.stem: A point falls beyond the upper control limit, but the part is within the specification. What is the right response?

options.html: Do nothing, because the part passes
Investigate the special cause before it grows, even though the part is acceptable

5.3.3-2.explanation: A point can signal a special cause while still within spec. Investigate it.

5.3.3-3.stem: The chart is stable, but 4% of output is out of specification. What is the correct response?

options.html: Investigate each point for a special cause
Improve or redesign the process (reduce variation or recenter), and contain nonconforming output meanwhile

5.3.3-3.explanation: A stable but incapable process needs a change to the process itself, not a hunt for special causes.

5.3.3-4.stem: Which TWO are normal elements of a response plan?

options.html: The trigger (the signal or rule that starts the plan)
Who acts and who is escalated to

5.3.3-4.explanation: A response plan lists the trigger, containment, who acts, investigation, corrective action, escalation, documentation, and how to resume.

5.3.3-5.stem: Product found out of specification during a response is first:

options.html: Segregated, then dispositioned (sort, rework, scrap, or accept as is) by someone with the authority to decide

5.3.3-5.explanation: The plan states who may decide the disposition. Segregation comes first.

5.3.1-1.text: Without controls, a project's $150,000 per year of savings is expected to erode by 40%. A control system costs $50,000 upfront plus $12,000 per year. Find the expected annual loss prevented, the annual net benefit, and the payback on the upfront cost. Is it justified?
5.3.1-1.answer: Expected loss = 0.4 × 150,000 = $60,000. Net annual benefit = 60,000 − 12,000 = $48,000. Payback = 50,000 ÷ 48,000 = 1.04 years (12.5 months). Justified.

5.3.1-2.text: Without controls, a project's $150,000 per year of savings is expected to erode by 50%. A control system costs $50,000 upfront plus $3,000 per year. Find the expected annual loss prevented, the annual net benefit, and the payback on the upfront cost. Is it justified?
5.3.1-2.answer: Expected loss = 0.5 × 150,000 = $75,000. Net annual benefit = 75,000 − 3,000 = $72,000. Payback = 50,000 ÷ 72,000 = 0.69 years (8.3 months). Justified.

5.3.1-3.text: Without controls, a project's $40,000 per year of savings is expected to erode by 40%. A control system costs $30,000 upfront plus $5,000 per year. Find the expected annual loss prevented, the annual net benefit, and the payback on the upfront cost. Is it justified?
5.3.1-3.answer: Expected loss = 0.4 × 40,000 = $16,000. Net annual benefit = 16,000 − 5,000 = $11,000. Payback = 30,000 ÷ 11,000 = 2.73 years (32.7 months). Justified.

5.3.1-4.text: Without controls, a project's $80,000 per year of savings is expected to erode by 25%. A control system costs $20,000 upfront plus $3,000 per year. Find the expected annual loss prevented, the annual net benefit, and the payback on the upfront cost. Is it justified?
5.3.1-4.answer: Expected loss = 0.25 × 80,000 = $20,000. Net annual benefit = 20,000 − 3,000 = $17,000. Payback = 20,000 ÷ 17,000 = 1.18 years (14.1 months). Justified.

5.3.1-5.text: Without controls, a project's $80,000 per year of savings is expected to erode by 40%. A control system costs $50,000 upfront plus $5,000 per year. Find the expected annual loss prevented, the annual net benefit, and the payback on the upfront cost. Is it justified?
5.3.1-5.answer: Expected loss = 0.4 × 80,000 = $32,000. Net annual benefit = 32,000 − 5,000 = $27,000. Payback = 50,000 ÷ 27,000 = 1.85 years (22.2 months). Justified.

5.3.1-6.text: Without controls, a project's $60,000 per year of savings is expected to erode by 40%. A control system costs $20,000 upfront plus $8,000 per year. Find the expected annual loss prevented, the annual net benefit, and the payback on the upfront cost. Is it justified?
5.3.1-6.answer: Expected loss = 0.4 × 60,000 = $24,000. Net annual benefit = 24,000 − 8,000 = $16,000. Payback = 20,000 ÷ 16,000 = 1.25 years (15.0 months). Justified.

5.3.1-7.text: A manual audit costs $20,000 per year and is expected to prevent $10,000 per year of losses. Is it justified, and what is the net effect per year?
5.3.1-7.answer: Net = 10,000 − 20,000 = $-10,000 per year. Not justified: it costs more than it protects.

5.3.1-8.text: A manual audit costs $12,000 per year and is expected to prevent $4,000 per year of losses. Is it justified, and what is the net effect per year?
5.3.1-8.answer: Net = 4,000 − 12,000 = $-8,000 per year. Not justified: it costs more than it protects.

5.3.1-9.text: A manual audit costs $6,000 per year and is expected to prevent $10,000 per year of losses. Is it justified, and what is the net effect per year?

5.3.1-10.text: A manual audit costs $20,000 per year and is expected to prevent $4,000 per year of losses. Is it justified, and what is the net effect per year?
5.3.1-10.answer: Net = 4,000 − 20,000 = $-16,000 per year. Not justified: it costs more than it protects.
